title: Why Is My Walk-In Cooler Not Cooling?
h1: Why is my walk-in cooler not cooling or holding temperature?
meta_desc: A warm walk-in cooler usually has one of six causes — and half cost nothing to fix. The checks to run before you pay for an emergency refrigeration call.
teaser: Six causes explain most warm walk-ins. Three of them are free to fix, and product is on the clock.
body_html:
A warm walk-in is a race against your inventory, so this list is ordered by speed: the fastest, cheapest checks first. Keep the door shut while you work through it — a full, closed box holds temperature for hours; an open one doesn't.

1. Check the controller for an alarm code — 30 seconds

If your box has a digital controller, it has probably already diagnosed itself. Heatcraft's intelliGen shows AL and ER codes, a Beacon II system shows A and E codes, KE2 Therm controllers scroll named alarms, and Dixell controllers on Norlake and Kolpak boxes show two-letter codes like HA (high temperature) or P1 (probe failure). Look the exact code up on this site before touching anything — it tells you whether the system is still trying to cool or has shut itself down, which changes everything about urgency.

2. The door — the number one cause, and it's free

A door propped open during a delivery, a torn or hard gasket, a sagging hinge, a latch that doesn't pull tight, a strip curtain that got tied back and never released — door problems cause more warm walk-ins than every mechanical failure combined. Check that the door actually seals: a dollar bill closed in the gasket should drag when you pull it. While you're there, check the door switch; a misaligned switch tells the controller the door is open and can shut fans down.

3. The evaporator coil — is it a block of ice?

Look at the coil unit inside the box. If it's buried in ice, air can't move through it and the box can't cool, no matter how healthy the refrigeration system is. Icing always has a cause — a failed defrost heater, a defrost schedule problem, a door leaking humid air, or a failed coil probe ending defrosts wrong — and melting it without fixing the cause buys you days, not a repair. Note it for the tech; don't chip at it.

4. The evaporator fans

Fans should run whenever the box is calling for cooling (some configurations stop them when the door opens). Fan blades not turning means no air across the coil — check the breaker, then look for ice binding the blades. Motor and contactor replacement is a service job.

5. The condensing unit — where the heat actually goes

Find the condensing unit (on the roof, out back, or on top of the box). Is it running? Is the coil clean, or matted with dust, lint, and grease? Is airflow blocked by stored boxes, a fence, or leaves? A dirty or suffocated condenser can't reject the box's heat — in summer it trips high-pressure safeties, and on Dixell-equipped units you may see the HA2 condenser alarm. Check its breaker too. Cleaning a condenser coil (power off first) is legitimate in-house maintenance.

6. What changed today?

Warm product loaded straight into the box, a big delivery with the door open twenty minutes, a deep-cleaning crew that unplugged something, a breaker tripped during a storm. Half of "broken" walk-ins are a normal box digesting an abnormal day. Give a loaded box time to recover — but log the temperature every 30 minutes while you wait, both for food safety and so you know if it's actually recovering.

When it's a real service call

Door sealing, coil clear, fans running, condenser clean and running, breakers on — and it's still warm? What's left is refrigerant charge, valves, and the compressor: licensed-technician territory, and worth calling fast because product loss usually costs more than the visit. If you're in Middle Tennessee or Central Alabama, start with the verified service lists for Nashville and Birmingham. Tell them the controller code, the box temperature and trend, and what you've already checked — that's the difference between one truck roll and two.

title: What Do Walk-In Cooler Alarm Codes Mean?
h1: What do the alarm codes on my walk-in cooler mean?
meta_desc: Walk-in cooler alarms come from the controller, not the box: Heatcraft intelliGen and Beacon II, KE2 Therm, Dixell, and Norlake panels each use different codes.
teaser: The box doesn't throw codes — the controller does. Identify yours and go straight to the right list.
body_html:
Here's the thing that trips people up when a walk-in starts alarming: the brand on the door — Norlake, Kolpak, or a local box builder — usually isn't the brand doing the talking. The box is insulation and panels. The alarms come from the refrigeration system and its controller, and a handful of controller families cover most of the commercial market. Identify which one you're looking at, and the code list follows.

Heatcraft intelliGen — AL, ER, and IN codes

Heatcraft (whose equipment sells under the Bohn and Larkin names) ships the intelliGen controller on current unit coolers: a small OLED display with a colored light bar. Red bar plus an AL code is an alarm — AL01 is high box temperature, AL06 the door alarm. Yellow plus an ER code is an error, usually a sensor — ER01 is the box temperature sensor. IN codes are informational. Newer A2L-refrigerant units add leak-detection alarms (AL12, ER32) that you should treat as evacuate-and-call events. Full Heatcraft list →

Heatcraft Beacon II — A and E codes

The previous generation of Heatcraft smart systems shows A1-A4 alarms and E1-E9 errors on the board display, with an optional Smart Controller LCD that flashes text like *BOXHI and +COMM+. The logic mirrors intelliGen: A1 high box temp, A4/E-codes for failed sensors — several of which pump the system down and keep it off until repaired, which makes them urgent. Full Beacon II list →

KE2 Therm — named, scrolling alarms

KE2 Evaporator Efficiency controllers don't use cryptic codes at all — they scroll names: HIGH AIR TEMP, DOOR SWITCH, EXCESS DEFROST, LOW SUPERHEAT. Yellow LED means the system is still running; a red-LED alarm like PRESSURE SENSOR means it shut down to protect the compressor and the clock is running on your product. Full KE2 list →

Dixell — the two-letter codes on Norlake, Kolpak and many others

The little Dixell (Emerson) XR-series thermostat is everywhere in walk-ins. Its codes are terse: P1-P4 are probe failures, HA/LA high and low temperature alarms, dA door alarm, EA/CA external alarms — with CA being the serious one that switches everything off. And the one that generates the most confused phone calls isn't a fault at all: OF/PoF just means the keypad is locked (hold up and down arrows for 3 seconds). Full Dixell list →

Norlake control panels — plain-text alarms

Norlake's programmable walk-in panels (built on Carel hardware) skip codes entirely and scroll plain text: DOOR AJAR ALARM, ROOM TEMP HIGH ALARM, AIR FLOW LOSS. Read them literally, silence with the ALARM button while you investigate, and check the status line for fallback modes like SENSOR FAIL MODE that mean the panel is limping on backup logic. Full Norlake list →

The universal rules, whatever the controller

  1. Photograph the display before resetting anything. The code plus the box temperature is your service call in one picture.
  2. Know whether the system is still running. A running system with a high-temp alarm is urgency measured in hours; a shut-down system is urgency measured in product.
  3. Log box temperature every 30 minutes during any event — for food safety compliance and for your own diagnosis.
  4. One reset is diagnosis. An alarm that returns is telling the truth; forcing restarts against a pressure or superheat fault is how compressors die.

When the code points past what staff can safely do, the verified service lists for Nashville and Birmingham cover contractors who work on all of these systems.

title: Why Is Ice Building Up in My Walk-In Freezer?
h1: Why is ice building up in my walk-in freezer or cooler?
meta_desc: Ice on the evaporator coil, ceiling, or door of a walk-in freezer always has a cause: defrost failure, door leaks, or drain problems. Find yours before it kills the compressor.
teaser: Every patch of ice in a walk-in is moisture that got in and a defrost that didn't handle it. Find the source.
body_html:
Ice in a walk-in freezer looks like a nuisance you chip away at. It's actually the box keeping a written record of a problem: every pound of ice is moisture that got in and a defrost system that couldn't keep up. Where the ice forms tells you what's wrong.

Ice on the evaporator coil — defrost isn't finishing its job

The evaporator naturally frosts during operation; the defrost cycle (electric heaters in a freezer) melts it off several times a day. A coil turning into a glacier means defrost is failing: burned-out heater elements, a failed defrost termination sensor ending cycles too early, a timer or controller problem, or simply not enough defrost cycles for how much moisture the box is taking in. Controllers document this — Heatcraft's intelliGen flags coil-sensor errors like ER02, Dixell's P2 probe failure makes defrosts end on time instead of temperature, and KE2 controllers log DEFR TERM ON TIME when two defrosts in a row can't reach termination temperature. An iced coil also blocks airflow — which is how an ice problem becomes a warm-box problem, and eventually a low-superheat condition that can flood liquid refrigerant back to the compressor. That's the expensive ending this article exists to prevent.

Ice around the door — the box is breathing humid air

Ice on the door frame, the ceiling just inside the door, or the floor at the threshold means outside air is getting in and dumping its moisture: a torn or hardened gasket, a door that doesn't self-close and latch, a failed frame heater on the freezer door letting the gasket freeze to the frame (and then get torn by the next person yanking it open), or simply a door that stands open through every delivery. Fixes here are cheap — gaskets, sweeps, door closers, strip curtains, staff habits — and they're the highest-return maintenance a walk-in gets, because every one of them also cuts the load on defrost and the compressor.

Ice under the coil or on the floor — the drain line froze

Defrost water has to leave the box through a drain line. In a freezer, that line is supposed to be heated and pitched; when the drain heater fails or the pitch is wrong, meltwater refreezes in the pan or the line, then overflows as sheet ice under the evaporator and puddles that become a skating rink. Floor ice is a slip injury and a health-inspection finding waiting to happen — treat a frozen drain as a real repair, not a mop-and-forget.

What staff can safely do

  • Fix the moisture sources: gaskets, closers, curtains, door discipline during deliveries.
  • Keep product from blocking the evaporator's airflow — cartons stacked into the air stream cause localized icing.
  • Log when and where ice reappears after a defrost — that pattern is diagnostic gold for the tech.
  • Don't chip ice off the coil with tools. Fins bend, tubes puncture, and a punctured evaporator turns a service call into a replacement.

When to call

Any recurring coil icing, any suspected heater or sensor failure, and any frozen drain: these involve live electrical heaters, refrigeration diagnosis, and controller settings — technician work. Check your controller's exact code first (Heatcraft, KE2 Therm, Dixell, Norlake), then — in our test markets — the verified contractor lists for Nashville and Birmingham are the shortcut to someone who's fixed this exact pattern a hundred times.

title: How Do You Maintain a Commercial Walk-In Cooler?
h1: How do you maintain a commercial walk-in cooler or freezer?
meta_desc: A daily, weekly, and quarterly maintenance rhythm for commercial walk-in coolers and freezers — built around the failures that actually take boxes down.
teaser: Walk-ins fail from neglect in predictable ways. A daily/weekly/quarterly rhythm that catches all of them early.
body_html:
A walk-in cooler is the only piece of kitchen equipment whose failure can wipe out five figures of inventory overnight and hand you a health-department problem in the same stroke. It's also one of the most predictable machines in the building: walk-ins fail from the same short list of neglected items, in the same order, every time. This checklist is that list, turned into a rhythm.

Daily — 60 seconds, whoever closes

  • Read the thermometer or controller display and write it down. A daily temperature log is your early-warning system and your food-safety documentation in one line of pencil. A box that's drifted two degrees warm at the same load tells you weeks before an alarm does.
  • Look for new alarm codes or lights. If there's a code, look it up the same day (Heatcraft, KE2, Dixell, Norlake) — yellow-level alarms caught early are the cheap ones.
  • Confirm the door closes and latches itself. No propping, no boxes in the threshold, strip curtains hanging free.

Weekly — 5 minutes

  • Check the door gasket with the dollar-bill test around all four sides; wipe gaskets clean so grime doesn't harden them.
  • Glance at the evaporator for frost patterns and listen to the fans. Uneven frost or a noisy fan bearing are both early tells.
  • Check the floor and pan area for water or ice — drainage problems announce themselves small.
  • Enforce airflow inside the box: nothing stacked against the evaporator intake or discharge, product off the floor.

Monthly — 15 minutes

  • Inspect the condensing unit (roof, back lot, or on top of the box): coil clean, airflow clear, no debris, fans turning. In a greasy or dusty environment this is the highest-value quarter hour in the building.
  • Test the door hardware honestly: hinges, closer tension, latch, and the door switch alignment. On freezer doors, confirm the frame heater is keeping the gasket from freezing to the frame.
  • Watch one defrost cycle end if your controller shows it — coils should come out clean.

Quarterly to semi-annual — the professional visit

  • Refrigerant charge and superheat verified with gauges
  • Defrost heaters, termination sensor, and schedule tested and tuned
  • Coils professionally cleaned (evaporator and condenser)
  • Drain line and drain heater verified, pan cleaned and sanitized
  • Controller setpoints, alarm limits, and sensor calibration checked against a reference thermometer
  • Electrical connections, contactors, and fan motors inspected

Every service company on our Nashville and Birmingham pages offers planned-maintenance agreements covering exactly this scope; for multi-box operations, per-fleet pricing is standard and worth negotiating.

The two habits that outperform everything else

First: the daily temperature log. It costs nothing, satisfies your health inspector, documents any insurance claim, and catches drift before it becomes an emergency. Second: same-day code lookups. Controllers announce failures early and specifically — a sensor error or excess-defrost alarm ignored for a month is how a $200 repair matures into a compressor replacement plus a full box of lost product. The machine is talking; the whole discipline is listening on the day it speaks.

title: How Cold Should a Walk-In Cooler or Freezer Be?
h1: How cold should a walk-in cooler or freezer be?
meta_desc: Walk-in coolers should hold food at 41°F or below per the FDA Food Code — most run 35-38°F air temperature. Freezers run 0°F or below. What the numbers mean and how to verify yours.
teaser: Coolers: food at 41°F or below, so most boxes run 35-38°F. Freezers: 0°F or below. Here's why, and how to check yours honestly.
body_html:
The short answer, then the reasoning. Walk-in coolers: the FDA Food Code requires cold food held at 41°F (5°C) or below, so most commercial walk-in coolers are set to hold air temperature around 35-38°F — cold enough that product stays under 41°F even through door traffic and defrost cycles, warm enough that nothing freezes. Walk-in freezers: frozen food should stay frozen solid, which in practice means 0°F or below, with ice cream operations often running colder (around -10°F) because ice cream scoops properly only when it's colder than most frozen goods need.

Why air temperature and product temperature aren't the same number

Your controller reads air temperature, and air swings: it jumps when the door opens, rises during every defrost, and dips as the system pulls back down. Product temperature moves much more slowly — a case of product barely notices a 15-minute door-open event that sends the air display up ten degrees. This is why health inspectors probe product, not air, and why one air-temperature spike on the display doesn't automatically mean unsafe food. What matters is the pattern: air that averages 36-38°F keeps product safely below 41°F; air that averages 44°F does not, no matter what the sticker on the door says.

Why not just run it colder?

Because both directions cost money. A cooler run at 33°F instead of 37°F freezes the lettuce, the berries, and the milk at the coldest spots near the evaporator discharge — product loss by overcooling is a real and common loss. It also runs the compressor harder for zero food-safety gain. On the freezer side, every degree below what your product actually requires is pure energy spend. Set the box to what the product needs, not to the coldest number the dial allows.

The numbers that trigger action

  • Cooler air consistently above 41°F: product is drifting toward the danger zone. Work the not-cooling checklist now and start logging temperatures.
  • Cooler product at 41°F+ for over 4 hours: the standard food-safety time-temperature threshold where product disposition becomes a real question. This is exactly the excursion that controllers with HACCP functions (Danfoss's A60 HACCP alarm, Carel's HA/HF events) log automatically.
  • Freezer creeping above ~10°F: product softens, quality degrades, and refreezing damages texture — investigate before it reaches thawing territory.

How to verify your box honestly

  1. Don't trust one thermometer. Verify the controller's reading against an independent thermometer placed mid-box, away from the door and the evaporator discharge. Controller probes drift, and several alarm codes on this site (Dixell P1, Danfoss E29, Carel E0) exist precisely because sensors fail.
  2. Log it daily. One line of pencil per day, same time every day. The log satisfies your inspector, documents any insurance claim, and shows drift weeks before a breakdown.
  3. Know your box's normal rhythm — its post-defrost peak, its door-rush spike, its pull-down speed. Alarms make sense only against a known normal.

When the temperature is right but the alarms aren't

If your independent thermometer says 37°F but the controller alarms high (or vice versa), the problem is the sensor or the alarm settings, not the refrigeration — look up the exact code (Heatcraft, KE2, Dixell, Danfoss, Carel, Norlake). And if the box genuinely can't hold its number, the verified service lists for Nashville and Birmingham are the next call.

title: Why Does My Walk-In Cooler Run Constantly?
h1: Why does my walk-in cooler run constantly and never shut off?
meta_desc: A walk-in compressor that never cycles off is either fighting a real heat load, starved by a system problem, or misled by a sensor. How to tell which — and what it's costing you.
teaser: A compressor that never cycles off is fighting heat, starving for refrigerant, or being lied to by a sensor.
body_html:
A healthy walk-in cycles: the compressor runs, the box reaches setpoint, the compressor rests. One that runs around the clock is telling you one of three stories — it's fighting more heat than it should, it's too weak to win, or it's being lied to. Each story has its own checks, and running constantly is expensive in every version: electricity burned around the clock, and compressor life consumed at double speed.

Story one: the box is gaining heat it shouldn't

The most common and cheapest-to-fix version. Heat sneaks in through:

  • Door problems — a torn or hardened gasket, a door that doesn't self-close, strip curtains tied back, or heavy traffic propping it open through every delivery. A walk-in door leaking air makes the compressor run to cool the whole kitchen.
  • Infiltration you can see: ice or condensation around the door frame is humid outside air writing you a note.
  • Warm product loading — cooling a rack of hot prep down in the walk-in forces hours of extra runtime. Pre-chill what you can.
  • Panel damage or failed insulation — wet, sagging, or damaged panels lose R-value permanently.

Fix the door and the habits first; they're free-to-cheap and they're the answer a surprising share of the time.

Story two: the system is too weak to reach setpoint

The box gains normal heat, but the refrigeration can't overcome it:

  • An iced evaporator coil blocks airflow — the system runs but moves no cold air. Ice always has a cause; see the ice buildup guide.
  • A filthy condenser can't reject heat — the classic summer version, and the one behind high-condenser alarms like Dixell's HA2, Danfoss's A61/A80, and Carel's cht/CHt codes. Cleaning the coil is legitimate in-house work.
  • Failed evaporator or condenser fans — cold made but not moved.
  • Low refrigerant charge — the system runs endlessly and never quite gets there. That diagnosis needs gauges and an EPA-certified tech, and it means there's a leak to find, not just gas to add.

Story three: the controller is being lied to

A temperature sensor that reads warm keeps calling for cooling forever — the box may actually be at 30°F and freezing product while the display insists it's 42°F. The tell: your independent thermometer disagrees with the display, or product near the evaporator starts freezing. Sensor failures are exactly what codes like Dixell P1, Danfoss E29, and Carel E0 announce — but a drifting sensor can lie without tripping any code, which is why the independent thermometer is the referee.

The order of operations

  1. Verify actual box temperature with an independent thermometer. At setpoint but still running? Suspect the sensor or settings. Above setpoint? Continue.
  2. Inspect the door, gaskets, and closing hardware. Fix what you find.
  3. Look at the evaporator (ice? fans running?) and the condenser (clean? fan running? airflow clear?). Clean the condenser — power off first.
  4. Ask what changed: warm loads, new door traffic, a heat wave, recent service.
  5. Still running constantly after all four? What remains — charge, valves, compressor wear — is instrument territory. In our test markets, the verified contractor lists for Nashville and Birmingham are the shortcut.

One honest warning: constant running is also how walk-ins die young. A compressor designed to cycle that instead runs 24/7 is aging on fast-forward — the electric bill is the visible cost, and the shortened compressor life is the bigger invisible one. This symptom rewards fixing early.

title: Why Is There Water on My Walk-In Cooler Floor?
h1: Why is there water on the floor of my walk-in cooler?
meta_desc: Water on a walk-in floor comes from four places: the defrost drain, door infiltration, the evaporator pan, or a real leak. How to trace it — before the slip-and-fall or the citation.
teaser: Four sources explain walk-in floor water: the drain, the door, the pan, or a leak. Trace it before the injury or the citation.
body_html:
Water on a walk-in floor is never just a mop job. It's a slip hazard in a room where staff carry heavy loads, a health-inspection finding, and — left standing — a floor-panel killer, because water that migrates into panel seams destroys insulation and rots floors from inside. The good news: floor water comes from a short list of sources, and where the water shows up tells you which one you have.

Source one: the condensate drain — the usual suspect

Every defrost cycle melts frost off the evaporator coil, and that water is supposed to leave through the drain pan and drain line. When it doesn't, it ends up on your floor:

  • A clogged drain line — slime, debris, or ice blocks the line and the pan overflows, dripping under the evaporator. Puddles directly below the coil unit point here.
  • A frozen drain line (freezers) — freezer drain lines need heat tape and proper pitch; when the drain heater fails, meltwater refreezes in the line, then the next defrost overflows the pan. The signature: ice stalactites under the coil and sheet ice on the floor beneath it.
  • Bad pitch or a trap problem — a line that sags holds water and eventually blocks. This is an installation flaw that presents as a recurring "clog."

Note that some controllers can relay a pan overflow float switch as an external alarm — KE2's EXT ALARM and Dixell's EA are commonly wired to exactly that.

Source two: the door — condensation and ice melt

Humid outside air sneaking past a bad gasket condenses and freezes around the door area; every warm spell or defrost melts some of it onto the threshold. Water or ice concentrated at the door end of the box is an air-leak finding, not a drain finding — and the fix (gaskets, sweeps, closer adjustment, door discipline) is cheap and also cuts your energy bill and your coil-icing problem at the same time.

Source three: sweating — the box working against humidity

In a humid kitchen, exterior panel surfaces and exposed cold lines can sweat, and floors just inside frequently-opened doors collect condensation from the air exchange. Persistent general dampness (rather than localized puddles) in summer points here. Ventilation around the box and door discipline are the levers; a box that sweats heavily year-round may have a panel losing its insulation value — worth a professional look.

Source four: an actual water leak

Walk-ins near dish pits, ice machines, or plumbing walls sometimes collect someone else's water. If the puddle doesn't map to the evaporator, the door, or humidity patterns — or it's there even in dry winter weeks — look uphill: what's on the other side of that wall or above the ceiling panels? Trace before assuming the cooler is the culprit.

The 10-minute trace

  1. Map the puddle. Under the evaporator = drain. At the door = infiltration. General dampness = humidity. Unrelated corner = external leak.
  2. Look up. Drips from the coil unit or pan confirm drain problems; ice on the ceiling near the door confirms infiltration.
  3. Check the drain outlet outside the box — a healthy drain visibly discharges after defrost.
  4. Fix the cheap causes now (clear the drain outlet, fix gaskets, mop and dry the seams), and get a tech for frozen drain lines, failed drain heaters, and pan repairs — those involve heaters and disassembly. The verified lists for Nashville and Birmingham cover contractors who handle exactly this.

And whatever the source: dry the floor completely and keep it dry. Standing water in a walk-in is the one problem on this site that injures people directly — everything else just costs money.
